## From first principles to writing your own tools

### PART I — Foundations · Modules 1–5

*The R mindset · vectors & strings · control flow · data structures · functions*

Read a section, then do the matching exercises in `PartI_exercises.R` before continuing.

## How to use Part I

This is the foundations half of the course. Five modules take you from “I can open RStudio” to “I can write structured R programs with my own functions, scripts I can `source()`, and the right data structure for each job.” The course is built for bioinformatics: every example is a sequence, a gene, a variant, or a results table.

The material comes in three files per part: this theory document, an **exercises** script (`PartI_exercises.R`), and a **solutions** script (`PartI_solutions.R`). The theory is broken into short sections. After most sections you will see a **▶ Practise now** box telling you which exercises to do before reading on. Do them in that order — alternating small theory with immediate practice is how programming sticks.

A note on philosophy. R is not Python with different punctuation. Its defining idea is the **vector**: almost everything is a vector, and almost every operation works on a whole vector at once. If you learn to *think in vectors* from day one, the rest of R — data frames, the tidyverse, Bioconductor — falls into place. Where this course shows you a loop, it will usually then show you the vectorised version you should prefer.

**Time guide.** Module 1 ≈ 3h · Module 2 ≈ 6h · Module 3 ≈ 4h · Module 4 ≈ 7h · Module 5 ≈ 6h. Total ≈ 26 hours including exercises. The exercises are where the learning happens.

## Chapter 0 — Your environment (do this first)

A wobbly setup is where most people stall before writing a line of real code. Get this working before Module 1.

### 0.1 Install R and RStudio

Two separate things:

-   **R** is the engine — the language and interpreter. Download it from CRAN (`https://cran.r-project.org`).
-   **RStudio Desktop** is the cockpit — the editor, console, plots pane, and environment viewer you actually work in. Download it from Posit (`https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/`).

Install R first, then RStudio; RStudio finds R automatically.

### 0.2 Use Projects, always

In RStudio, choose **File → New Project → New Directory** and make one called `r-bioinformatics`. A Project sets the working directory to that folder, so file paths like `"data/sample.fasta"` just work, and it keeps each piece of work self-contained. Put the course `data/` folder inside your project folder.

### 0.3 Three ways to run R

1.  **The console** (bottom-left pane) — type an expression, press Enter, see the result. Good for quick checks.
2.  **A script** (`.R` file) — write code, run a line with **Ctrl/Cmd+Enter**, or the whole file with **source**. This is where real work lives; it is what the exercises are.
3.  **R Markdown / Quarto** — prose and code together, for reports (Part V).

### 0.4 A sanity check

Open a new script, type this, and run it:

    R.version.string
    print("ready")

If you see your R version and `"ready"`, you are set.

## Module 1 — Setup, syntax & the R mindset

Estimated: 3 hours. This module is about R’s way of expressing the basics, and the handful of places it will surprise you.

### 1.1 Assignment: `<-` is the R way

R assigns with the arrow `<-`:

    gene_name <- "rpoB"
    length_bp <- 3534L

`=` also works for assignment, but the convention — and what you will see in all R code — is `<-`. Keep `=` for naming arguments inside function calls (`read.csv("x.csv", header = TRUE)`), where it means something different. RStudio types the arrow for you with **Alt/Option + minus**.

### 1.2 Everything is a vector

This is the single most important idea in R. There is no separate “single number” type — a lone value is just a vector of length 1.

    x <- 42
    length(x)   # 1  — it was a vector all along

You build longer vectors with `c()` (“combine”):

    lengths_bp <- c(3534, 2223, 2628)
    genes      <- c("rpoB", "katG", "gyrA")

And operations apply to the **whole vector at once** — no loop needed. This is *vectorisation*:

    lengths_bp / 3        # 1178 741 876   — divides every element
    lengths_bp > 2500     # TRUE FALSE TRUE
    paste0(genes, "_v2")  # "rpoB_v2" "katG_v2" "gyrA_v2"

If you came from Python, resist the urge to loop over elements. In R, the loop is already inside the operator.

### 1.3 The core types

R has four everyday atomic types:

  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Type                    Example                 Notes
  ----------------------- ----------------------- ------------------------------------------
  `double` (numeric)      `0.5237`, `3534`        the default for numbers, even whole ones

  `integer`               `3534L`                 the `L` suffix forces an integer

  `character`             `"rpoB"`                strings, in single or double quotes

  `logical`               `TRUE`, `FALSE`         also `T`/`F`, but prefer the full words
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Check and convert with the `is.*` / `as.*` families:

    class(3534)            # "numeric"
    is.numeric(3534)       # TRUE
    as.integer("2223")     # 2223  — string to integer
    as.numeric("4502300")  # 4502300

A vector holds **one type only**. Mix types and R silently *coerces* them all to the most flexible one (logical → integer → double → character):

    c(1, 2, "three")   # "1" "2" "three"  — all became character

This quiet coercion is a classic source of bugs — a stray text value turns your whole numeric column into text.

### 1.4 Missing values: `NA`

R has a first-class missing-value marker, `NA`. It is not zero and not an empty string; it means “unknown”. It is contagious — most calculations touching `NA` return `NA`:

    quality <- c(45.2, NA, 52.1)
    mean(quality)              # NA
    mean(quality, na.rm = TRUE)# 48.65  — drop NAs first
    is.na(quality)             # FALSE TRUE FALSE

You will meet `NA` constantly in real data. Learn `na.rm = TRUE` and `is.na()` now.

### 1.5 Output: `print`, `cat`, and `sprintf`

    print(gene_name)                     # the console default
    cat("Gene:", gene_name, "\n")        # concatenates with spaces, no quotes
    sprintf("GC = %.2f%%", 52.37)        # C-style formatting: "GC = 52.37%"

`sprintf()` is R’s equivalent of a Python f-string for formatted numbers: `%d` integer, `%f` float (`%.2f` = 2 decimals), `%s` string. The **glue** package (Part III) gives an even cleaner `glue("GC = {gc}")` style.

## Module 2 — Vectors & strings

Estimated: 6 hours. Strings in bioinformatics *are* sequences, so this module is central. In R, strings live in character vectors, and you manipulate them with functions (not methods).

### 2.1 Indexing starts at 1

R is **1-based**: the first element is `[1]`, not `[0]`.

    genes <- c("rpoB", "katG", "gyrA", "pncA")
    genes[1]            # "rpoB"   first
    genes[length(genes)]# "pncA"   last
    genes[c(1, 3)]      # "rpoB" "gyrA"   several
    genes[2:4]          # "katG" "gyrA" "pncA"   a range (inclusive both ends)

**Negative indices drop elements** (they do *not* count from the end, as in Python):

    genes[-1]     # "katG" "gyrA" "pncA"   — everything EXCEPT the first
    genes[-c(1,2)]# "gyrA" "pncA"

You can also index with a logical mask — keep the `TRUE` positions:

    lengths_bp <- c(3534, 2223, 2628, 561)
    lengths_bp[lengths_bp > 2000]   # 3534 2223 2628

### 2.2 Named vectors — a quick lookup

Give elements names and index by name — a lightweight dictionary:

    gc <- c(rpoB = 0.442, katG = 0.733, gyrA = 0.509)
    gc["katG"]   # 0.733
    names(gc)    # "rpoB" "katG" "gyrA"

### 2.3 The string toolbox

Base R string functions, with their most common uses:

    seq <- "ATGCGTACG"
    nchar(seq)                 # 9        — length in characters (NOT length())
    toupper("atgc")            # "ATGC"
    substr(seq, 1, 3)          # "ATG"    — characters 1 to 3 (1-based, inclusive)
    substring(seq, 4)          # "CGTACG" — from position 4 to the end
    paste(genes, collapse=",") # "rpoB,katG,gyrA,pncA"  — join a vector into one string
    strsplit("A,C,G,T", ",")   # splits into a list: c("A","C","G","T")
    gsub("T", "U", seq)        # "AUGCGUACG"  — replace ALL T with U (transcription)
    sub("T", "U", seq)         # replaces only the FIRST match
    grepl("ATG", seq)          # TRUE  — does the pattern occur?

Note `nchar()` for string length versus `length()` for vector length — a frequent beginner trip. `"ATGCGT"` is one element; its `length()` is 1 but its `nchar()` is 6.

The **stringr** package (tidyverse) wraps all of this in consistent `str_*` names — `str_length`, `str_sub`, `str_replace_all`, `str_detect` — which many people find easier to remember. We use base R here so you know what stringr is built on; feel free to prefer stringr later.

### 2.4 Counting bases and GC content

Because operations are vectorised, GC content falls out neatly. Split the sequence into single characters, then count:

    seq <- "ATGCGCGTAT"
    bases <- strsplit(seq, "")[[1]]   # c("A","T","G","C",...)
    table(bases)                       # A C G T  → 2 3 3 2  (a frequency table)
    gc <- sum(bases %in% c("G", "C")) / length(bases)
    gc   # 0.5

`%in%` tests membership element-by-element and returns a logical vector; `sum()` of a logical vector counts the `TRUE`s (because `TRUE` is 1). That idiom — `sum(condition)` to count matches — is everywhere in R.

### 2.5 The reverse complement

A good test of vectorised thinking. Complement each base, then reverse:

    revcomp <- function(seq) {
      bases <- strsplit(toupper(seq), "")[[1]]
      comp  <- c(A="T", T="A", G="C", C="G")[bases]  # named-vector lookup, vectorised
      paste(rev(comp), collapse = "")                 # rev() reverses, paste() rejoins
    }
    revcomp("ATGC")   # "GCAT"

The trick is `c(A="T", ...)[bases]`: indexing a named vector *by a vector of names* looks up every base at once — no loop. `rev()` reverses any vector. This is the idiomatic R reverse complement.

## Module 3 — Control flow & vectorised thinking

Estimated: 4 hours. R has the usual `if`/`for`/`while`, but the module’s real lesson is: **in R you reach for a loop far less often than in Python.** Learn the control-flow syntax, then learn the vectorised alternatives you should usually prefer.

### 3.1 Conditionals: `if` / `else if` / `else`

    gc <- 0.35
    if (gc > 0.6) {
      print("GC-rich")
    } else if (gc < 0.4) {
      print("AT-rich")
    } else {
      print("balanced")
    }

`if` takes a **single** `TRUE`/`FALSE`, not a vector. The condition goes in `( )`, the body in `{ }`. Combine conditions with `&&` and `||` (the scalar operators) in an `if`:

    if (length_bp > 1000 && gc >= 0.4 && gc <= 0.6) print("long and balanced")

### 3.2 Vectorised conditionals: `ifelse` and `case_when`

When you want to apply a condition to a *whole vector*, do not loop — use `ifelse()`, which returns a vector:

    gc <- c(0.35, 0.55, 0.72)
    ifelse(gc > 0.6, "high", "low")   # "low" "low" "high"

For several conditions, `dplyr::case_when()` (Part III) is the clean choice:

    dplyr::case_when(
      gc > 0.6  ~ "GC-rich",
      gc < 0.4  ~ "AT-rich",
      TRUE      ~ "balanced"
    )

Use `&` and `|` (single symbols) for vectorised logic like this; use `&&`/`||` only inside a scalar `if`.

### 3.3 Loops: `for` and `while`

A `for` loop iterates over the elements of a vector or list:

    for (g in genes) {
      cat("gene:", g, "\n")
    }

When you need an index, iterate over `seq_along()` (safe even for empty vectors — unlike `1:length(x)`):

    for (i in seq_along(genes)) {
      cat(i, "->", genes[i], "\n")
    }

A `while` loop runs until its condition is false — use it when you don’t know the count ahead of time, such as walking codons until a stop:

    cds <- "ATGAAACCCTAA"
    i <- 1
    while (i <= nchar(cds) - 2) {
      codon <- substr(cds, i, i + 2)
      if (codon %in% c("TAA", "TAG", "TGA")) { cat("stop at", i, "\n"); break }
      i <- i + 3
    }

`break` exits the loop; `next` skips to the next iteration (Python’s `continue`).

### 3.4 Prefer vectorisation

The GC loop you *could* write:

    seq <- "ATGCGCGTAT"; bases <- strsplit(seq, "")[[1]]
    gc <- 0
    for (b in bases) if (b == "G" || b == "C") gc <- gc + 1

…is better written as one vectorised line:

    gc <- sum(bases %in% c("G", "C"))

Shorter, faster, and harder to get wrong. The rule of thumb: **if you are looping to build up a number or a vector element-by-element, there is usually a vectorised function (**`sum`**,** `mean`**,** `cumsum`**,** `ifelse`**,** `table`**, the** `apply` **family in Part III) that does it in one call.**

## Module 4 — Data structures

Estimated: 7 hours. The payoff module. R’s data structures — especially the **data frame** — are what make it a data-analysis language. Choosing the right one is half of writing good R.

### 4.1 Vectors — the atom

Covered already: ordered, one type, 1-based, vectorised. Your default for a single column of values.

### 4.2 Lists — ordered, any types

A `list` holds elements of *different* types and lengths — including other lists. It is R’s general container.

    record <- list(gene = "rpoB", length = 3534L, gc = 0.442, exons = c(1, 2, 3))
    record$gene        # "rpoB"        — access by name with $
    record[["length"]] # 3534          — or with [[ ]]
    record["gc"]       # a one-element LIST (single brackets keep the list wrapper)

The `[[ ]]` vs `[ ]` distinction matters: `[[ ]]` extracts the *element*; `[ ]` returns a *sub-list*. Functions that return several results usually return a list (Module 5).

### 4.3 Factors — categories (an R speciality)

A `factor` stores a categorical variable: the values plus the set of allowed **levels**. This has no direct Python-beginner equivalent, and it matters because statistics and plots treat factors specially.

    condition <- factor(c("control", "treated", "control", "treated"))
    levels(condition)   # "control" "treated"
    table(condition)    # control 2  treated 2

Factors are great for fixed category sets (treatment groups, chromosomes). The trap: a factor *looks* like text but is stored as integers with labels, so converting back needs care — `as.numeric(factor("10"))` gives the level’s code, not `10`. Modern `readr` keeps strings as character by default and you make factors deliberately, which avoids most surprises.

### 4.4 Matrices — 2D, one type

A `matrix` is a vector folded into rows and columns, all one type. Useful for numeric grids (expression matrices, distance matrices):

    m <- matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)      # fills by column by default
    dim(m)                           # 2 3
    m[1, ]                           # first row
    m[, 2]                           # second column
    rowSums(m); colMeans(m)          # fast whole-row / whole-column summaries

### 4.5 Data frames — the workhorse

A `data.frame` is a list of equal-length vectors shown as a table: each column a vector (its own type), each row an observation. This is R’s equivalent of a pandas DataFrame, and it is where most bioinformatics data lives.

    variants <- data.frame(
      gene     = c("rpoB", "katG", "gyrA"),
      position = c(1349, 944, 248),
      quality  = c(45.2, 38.7, 52.1)
    )
    variants$gene            # a column (a vector)
    variants[variants$quality > 40, ]   # rows passing a filter
    nrow(variants); ncol(variants); names(variants)
    str(variants)            # structure: columns, types, samples

A **tibble** (tidyverse, Part III) is a modern data frame with nicer printing and no surprise factor conversion; everything you learn here applies to it.

### 4.6 Choosing the right structure

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Need                                                  Use
  ----------------------------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  A single column of same-type values                   **vector**

  A fixed set of categories                             **factor**

  Mixed types bundled together (a function’s results)   **list**

  A numeric grid, matrix maths                          **matrix**

  A table: rows = observations, columns = variables     **data frame / tibble**
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Module 5 — Functions, scope & scripts

Estimated: 6 hours. Functions turn loose commands into reusable tools. By the end you will have written your own sequence-analysis functions and split them into a file you can load from anywhere.

### 5.1 Defining and calling functions

A function is created with `function(...)` and (usually) assigned a name. The value of the **last expression** is returned automatically — an explicit `return()` is optional and used mainly for early exits.

    gc_content <- function(seq) {
      bases <- strsplit(toupper(seq), "")[[1]]
      sum(bases %in% c("G", "C")) / length(bases)   # last expression = return value
    }
    gc_content("ATGCGC")   # 0.6667

### 5.2 Arguments: positional, named, default

Arguments can be matched by position or by name, and can have defaults:

    count_base <- function(seq, base = "G") {
      bases <- strsplit(toupper(seq), "")[[1]]
      sum(bases == toupper(base))
    }
    count_base("ATGCGC")            # 2   — uses default base = "G"
    count_base("ATGCGC", base = "A")# 1   — named argument

Naming arguments makes calls readable and order-independent — prefer it for anything beyond the first obvious argument.

### 5.3 Returning multiple values

R functions return one object, so to return several things, bundle them in a **list**:

    analyse <- function(seq) {
      seq <- toupper(seq)
      bases <- strsplit(seq, "")[[1]]
      list(
        length = nchar(seq),
        gc     = sum(bases %in% c("G", "C")) / length(bases),
        valid  = all(bases %in% c("A", "C", "G", "T"))
      )
    }
    res <- analyse("ATGCGX")
    res$gc       # access by name
    res$valid    # FALSE — contains an X

`all()` returns `TRUE` only if every element is `TRUE`; `any()` is its partner. Both are vectorised tests you will use constantly for validation.

### 5.4 Scope: local by default

Variables created inside a function are **local** — they vanish when the function returns and do not clobber outside names:

    x <- 10
    f <- function() { x <- 99; x }
    f()   # 99  (the local x)
    x     # 10  (unchanged)

A function *can read* outside (global) variables if it doesn’t have its own, but relying on that makes code fragile. Pass what you need in as arguments; return what you produce. Avoid writing to globals from inside functions.

### 5.5 Scripts and `source()`

Real projects split code across files. Put reusable functions in their own script — say `seqtools.R` — and load them with `source()`:

    # --- seqtools.R ---
    gc_content <- function(seq) {
      bases <- strsplit(toupper(seq), "")[[1]]
      sum(bases %in% c("G", "C")) / length(bases)
    }
    revcomp <- function(seq) {
      comp <- c(A="T", T="A", G="C", C="G")[strsplit(toupper(seq), "")[[1]]]
      paste(rev(comp), collapse = "")
    }
    # --- in your analysis script ---
    source("seqtools.R")      # runs the file; functions now available
    gc_content("ATGCGC")      # 0.6667

This is the seed of a package. In Part V you will wrap functions like these into a real, installable R package with documentation and tests — the “put it on GitHub” capstone.

### 5.6 Where Part I leaves you

You can now: think in vectors; write conditionals and loops (and know when to vectorise instead); choose among vectors, lists, factors, matrices, and data frames; and write your own functions and load them from a script. In Part II we read real FASTA/FASTQ/CSV files, add error handling and automated tests, and build your own S3 classes — turning these loose functions into a trustworthy toolkit.
